name: Akoye
catalog_citation: Whitney, Henry (data checked by, October 1992). Organised Phonology Data: Akoye (Angoya, Akoyi, Lohiki, Obi) Language [MIW], Gulf Province. SIL, Papua New Guinea. PDF via Wayback Machine copy (20160304) of http://www-01.sil.org/pacific/png/pubs/928474531301/A…
catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress seems to be predictably assigned to the last vowel of the stem or first vowel of suffixes on stems with no vowel. Adverbs take penultimate stress. But there are exceptions to these rules. There are some contrasts for tone: pää [pɑɑ́] 'bird sp.' ... pää [pɑ̀ɑ] 'body' ... agana [ə̀ɡənə] 'sky' ... agana [əɡə́nə] 'lid' ... Beyond that we have little knowledge of the tone system.

audit.recode_to: Keep kind=morphological (stem-final accent). Re-cite to Whitney & Whitney 2000 §3.5.1 pp. 14-16 and refine prule: accent (high pitch + loudness) on the final stem vowel in nouns and verbs; stemless nouns/adjectives and IMPF/GNOM-prefixed verbs accent the first suffix vowel, PF a- prefixed verbs accent the prefix; /ə/ is skipped (accent on rightmost non-mid-central stem vowel; initial syllable if all later nuclei are /ə/); transitivizer ma- pulls accent left and several suffixes pull it right; 'many exceptions'; pitch contrastive only in a few noun pairs. Drop the hedge-based caution ('seems') since the 2000 source states the rule without it; the OPD's 'adverbs penultimate' line is not repeated in 2000 and should be attributed to the OPD only.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding OPD passage is verbatim on p. 3 of the held at the stated lines. (2) The deciding source is a 1992 SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (5 pp., one hedged sentence on stress). Glottolog lists only Whitney & Whitney 1991 Grammar Essentials; SIL-PNG also published Whitney & Whitney 2000 Akoye Phonology Essentials (48 pp.), which is the best available account. (3) Both fetched sources now via Wayback (sil.org is Cloudflare-blocked): the 2000 Phonology Essentials §3.5.1 confirms the stem-final morphological accent rule and refines it (schwa avoidance, prefix accent in perfective forms, accent-attracting affixes, compounds, 'many exceptions', marginal pitch contrast); the 1991 grammar's phonology overview is silent on stress placement. sources.quote: 'Accent is marked by high pitch, increased loudness, and sometimes by length. Pitch is contrastive in some environments (Table 13 [pä/pé 'skin, body', 'bird sp.', 'fish' sg/pl]), but is not productive in the language as a whole. Generally, accent is placed on the final vowel of the stem ... in nouns (10) and in verbs (11), though there are many exceptions to this generalization. If there is no vowel in the stem of a noun or adjective, the accent falls on the first vowel of the suffix. ... In n- (IMPF) and na- (GNOM) prefixed forms, the accent occurs on the suffix. sources.quote: Phoneme chart and post-vocalic voicing only; no stress-placement rule. Only prosodic remark (p. 6): 'There is also a productive rule that changes /a/ to /ə/ [scanned-uncertain vowels] in certain stressed environments. This may be something to do with pitch accent. We do not know what causes it, so we simply write whatever the surface form is.'
